rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some say the 309 years report the People of the Book’s reckoning, not necessarily the youths’ actual time in the cave; verse 26 then reserves knowledge to God.
rows.anchor: said by some to be God’s informing the Prophet of the number of years the People of the Book say they remained in the cave

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Others take 309 years as the youths’ actual sleep in the cave and understand God knows best to concern the interval after their death, shortly after discovery.
rows.anchor: Others claim that this figure represents the actual number of years the youths slept in the cave

rows.speaker: still others
rows.claim: Still others say 309 is the actual duration and settles the dispute about how long they remained.
rows.anchor: Still others suggest that the figure of 309 years represents the actual number of years in the cave

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some explain 300 years by the solar calendar plus nine years to express the same period in the lunar calendar used by the Prophet and Arabs.
rows.anchor: 300 years represents the amount of time they slept in the cave according to the solar calendar, and another 9 years would have to be added

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Unseen belongs to God alone, who alone knows it; the commentary supports this with several verses describing His knowledge of hidden things.
rows.anchor: The Unseen belongs to God alone

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exclamation means that no one sees or hears like God or better than Him, who is the Hearing and the Seeing.
rows.anchor: How well He sees, how well He hears is an exclamation indicating that none sees or hears like or better than God

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: One reported reading takes “they” to mean the youths of the cave, who have no protector except God.
rows.anchor: either the youths of the cave (R) or those who disputed about their affair (R)—have no protector but God

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Another reported reading takes “they” to mean those disputing about the youths’ affair, who have no protector except God.
rows.anchor: either the youths of the cave (R) or those who disputed about their affair (R)—have no protector but God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s judgment is final, with no appeal or revision.
rows.anchor: His Judgment is final and that there is no appeal to or revision of it

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: In context, God’s statement about the youths and how long they slept may itself be the final judgment on the matter.
rows.anchor: it may mean that His statement about the youths of the cave and the length of time they slept

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse answers Makkan demands for a different or altered Quran by instructing the Prophet to recite what was revealed.
rows.anchor: The Makkans, who were displeased by the Quran revealed to the Prophet, used to ask him to bring a different Quran or to alter it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: None alters God’s words; only God can replace one revelation with another.
rows.anchor: Only God can alter His revelations, replacing one with another

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse responds to prominent Makkans who would listen only if the Prophet sent away his poorer followers, and commands him to stay with sincere believers.
rows.anchor: some prominent Makkans indicated that they were willing to sit and listen to the Prophet’s teachings, but they wanted the Prophet’s poorer followers to leave

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling upon God includes invoking, praising and glorifying Him, supplication, and performing prayers.
rows.anchor: by invoking Him, praising and glorifying Him, supplicating Him, and performing their prayers

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Morning and evening may specify the times of invocation or describe its constant practice.
rows.anchor: may mean that they do so at these times specifically or that they do so constantly

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Seeking God’s Face means seeking to please Him and earn His reward instead of earthly benefits; at the highest mystical level it can mean seeking a vision of God.
rows.anchor: seeking to please God and earn His Reward rather than earthly rewards or benefits

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet must not look past the poor followers toward wealthier, influential potential followers or prefer the prominent over sincere, pious people.
rows.anchor: not to look past them toward other potential followers who may be wealthier or more influential

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet reportedly thanked God for letting him live until commanded to be patient with some men of his community.
rows.anchor: Praise be to God, Who did not let me die before commanding my soul to be patient with some men among my community

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The heedless person refers to the Makkans seeking the dismissal of the poorer followers.
rows.anchor: The one whose heart We have made heedless refers to the Makkans who wished the Prophet to drive away his poorer followers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their excess means prodigality, waste, and negligence, putting petty desires before truth.
rows.anchor: they are prodigal, wasteful, and negligent, putting their own petty desires before the truth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse is also associated with the incident in verse 28, when prominent Makkans sought to exclude poor believers.
rows.anchor: This verse is also said to have been revealed in connection with the incident described in v. 28

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Believe or disbelieve” is a warning, not permission to reject; the Prophet declares truth but does not determine acceptance, which ultimately belongs to God.
rows.anchor: Whosoever will, let him believe, and whosoever will, let him disbelieve is meant as a warning

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: One view says acceptance or rejection ultimately lies with God.
rows.anchor: This is a matter that lies ultimately with God

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Another view frames the choice from the human perspective: each person chooses whether to follow truth or turn away.
rows.anchor: from the human point of view, with the individual, who must choose whether to follow the truth or turn away from it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning is confirmed by the Hell punishment described in the latter half of the verse.
rows.anchor: the lines in the second half of the verse, which recount the horrors of Hell that have been prepared for the wrongdoers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The canopies of Fire surround wrongdoers on every side, above and below.
rows.anchor: the Fire will surround them from all sides, from above and below

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The molten-like liquid may be poured on Hell’s inhabitants or made them drink; here it is both poured on them and an evil drink.
rows.anchor: In the present verse, the water like molten lead is both showered on those in Hell and made an evil drink for them

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some picture a wall of water poured into Hell; when its inhabitants seek relief by drinking, its heat burns their faces.
rows.anchor: a wall of water poured down into Hell, and when those in Hell seek to drink from it to seek relief, the heat of the water burns their faces

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hell’s boiling and freezing drinks contrast with the Garden’s pleasant drinks.
rows.anchor: The evil drinks of Hell—both boiling and freezing cold—are meant to contrast with the exceedingly pleasant drinks of the Garden

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faces stand for persons as a whole in descriptions of punishment, rather than only the body part.
rows.anchor: faces being symbolic here of persons as a whole, rather than merely indicating a part of their bodies

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mā shāʾ Allāh recognizes that nothing happens outside God’s will.
rows.anchor: nothing happens outside of God’s Will; see 7:188, where the Prophet is told to say

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lā quwwata illā bi’Llāh acknowledges that no one accomplishes anything without God’s help.
rows.anchor: no individual can accomplish anything without the Help of God (R)

rows.speaker: Ibn Kathīr
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr says the verse grounds the custom of saying both formulas when pleased by good fortune; the second is also used amid distress.
rows.anchor: According to Ibn Kathīr, this verse is the source of the Muslim religious custom of saying, whenever one is pleased by some good fortune

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: A hadith identifies the latter formula, or lā ḥawla wa lā quwwata illā bi’Llāh, as among the treasures of the Garden.
rows.anchor: as among the “treasures of the Garden” (IK)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believer hopes God may give him something better than the disbeliever’s garden, in this world or the Hereafter; the Hereafter is better for the reverent.
rows.anchor: expresses his hope that God may well give him something better than the gardens of the disbeliever, either in this world or in the Hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The threatened reckoning from the sky is punishment from above; some interpret it as thunderbolts, perhaps with a torrential storm that destroys the garden and leaves barren earth.
rows.anchor: thunderbolts(ṣawāʾiq; Bḍ, R, Z), suggesting a torrential storm or rain that will wash away his trees and crops

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “His fruit was encompassed” can mean he lost all his wealth.
rows.anchor: His fruit was encompassed—that is, by ruin—meaning either that he lost all his wealth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, his garden was unexpectedly destroyed as his believing brother had warned.
rows.anchor: or that his garden was destroyed unexpectedly as his believing brother had warned him in vv. 40–41

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wringing his hands expresses remorse and regret.
rows.anchor: Upon seeing this he began to wring his hands as a gesture of remorse and regret

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Despite his earlier boast of having more men, the ruined disbeliever has no party to help him apart from God and cannot help himself.
rows.anchor: Despite the disbeliever’s earlier boasts that he was stronger in men than his brother (v. 34)

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: A different punctuation makes “there” describe the disbeliever’s helplessness, then states that protection belongs to God.
rows.anchor: can be punctuated differently to read

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Walāyah means protection, which ultimately belongs to God alone as Protector, especially for believers.
rows.anchor: Protection translates walāyah, and it belongs to God alone, ultimately, since God is the Walī, “Protector”

rows.speaker: scholars
rows.claim: The unvoweled text permits walāyah, denoting closeness and protection, or wilāyah, more often denoting authority; scholars differ on the intended reading.
rows.anchor: Walāyah here can also be read as wilāyah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ḥaqq is a Divine Name meaning the Real or True, especially favored in philosophical and mystical writings.
rows.anchor: The Real translates al-ḥaqq, which could also be rendered

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some take al-ḥaqq as an adjective for protection, yielding “true protection belongs to God.”
rows.anchor: some suggest that al-ḥaqq in this verse can be read as an adjective describing protection

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This parable restates the lesson of verses 32–44: worldly life depends on divine beneficence, flourishes through God’s power and mercy, then becomes lifeless chaff.
rows.anchor: This parable recapitulates the moral lessons of the longer parable

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The chaff image recalls the disbeliever’s flourishing gardens ending as a barren plain and resembles other Quranic parables.
rows.anchor: This imagery evokes the gardens of the disbeliever in the earlier parable, which flourish seemingly without end through God’s Provision

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The greatest losers are those who disbelieve in God’s signs and meeting Him, because their worldly efforts are futile.
rows.anchor: Those who disbelieve in the signs of their Lord, and in the meeting with Him (v. 105) are described in this passage as the greatest losers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They consider their work virtuous, as other verses say the deeds of disbelievers and wrongdoers seem fair to them.
rows.anchor: Such people reckon that they are virtuous in their works, for as mentioned in several verses the deeds of the disbelievers and wrongdoers seem fair to them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their deeds come to nothing because they disbelieve; deeds without faith are assigned no weight.
rows.anchor: their deeds have come to naught, because they are disbelievers, and deeds without faith are assigned no weight

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another verse compares the deeds of those who deny their prophets to scattered dust.
rows.anchor: In 25:23, it is said that the deeds of those who are guilty of denying their prophets will be as scattered dust

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maryam is Makkan and believed revealed after Fāṭir, though some report verses 58 and 71 as Madinan.
rows.anchor: is a Makkan sūrah believed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah is named for Mary, the only female figure named in a surah and the only woman named in the Quran.
rows.anchor: This is the only sūrah named for a female figure, and indeed Mary has the distinction of being the only woman mentioned by name in the Quran

rows.speaker: Ibn Ḥazm and Rūzbihān al-Baqlī
rows.claim: A small minority, including Ibn Ḥazm and Rūzbihān al-Baqlī, regards Mary as a female prophet because she receives revelation from Gabriel and named Quranic figures are generally prophets.
rows.anchor: the Andalusian theologian Ibn Ḥazm (d. 456/1064) and the Persian Sufi Rūzbihān al-Baqlī

rows.speaker: most Muslim authorities
rows.claim: Most authorities reject Mary’s prophethood because the Quran does not explicitly call her a prophet and tradition generally holds prophets to be male; she is instead an exceptionally pious woman of the highest rank among women.
rows.anchor: most Muslim authorities do not consider Mary a prophet, but rather an exceptionally pious woman with the highest spiritual rank among women

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: A hadith names Mary among the four spiritually perfected women of the world.
rows.anchor: In a ḥadīth, the Prophet names Mary as one of the four spiritually perfected women of the world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mary uniquely connects Islam, Judaism, and Christianity: born to a priestly Jewish family and dedicated to the Temple, she is Jesus’ mother and central to Christianity; the Quran gives her story substantial detail.
rows.anchor: Mary represents a unique point of connection between Islam, Judaism, and Christianity

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After Badr, Makkan leaders asked the Negus to surrender Muslims sheltered in Abyssinia; Jaʿfar recited this surah, and the king and court wept and refused.
rows.anchor: Upon hearing the Quran’s words regarding Mary and Jesus, the Negus and the religious leaders of his court began to weep profusely and refused to hand over the Muslims

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah has a prominent rhyme pattern: 67 of 98 verses share a final sound, with shorter passages using separate related patterns.
rows.anchor: sixty-seven of its ninety-eight verses end with the same final sound

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Raḥmān is used repeatedly and most commonly as the Divine Name here; nearly a third of its Quranic occurrences outside the basmalah are in this surah.
rows.anchor: nearly a third of all instances of this Divine Name in the Quran (i.e., other than in the opening basmalah formula) are located in this sūrah alone

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accounts of Zachariah, Mary, Abraham, and Moses pair divine gifts of prophetic children or relatives with each figure’s withdrawal from their people and worldly separation.
rows.anchor: In all four accounts these Divine “gifts” are granted only after Zachariah, Mary, Abraham, and Moses withdraw from their people and enter a state of separation from the world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zachariah and Mary’s temporary silences are paired with the infant Jesus’ miraculous speech.
rows.anchor: Zachariah and Mary’s temporary silence (vv. 10–11, 26) is complemented

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the Ishmael and Idrīs accounts, the surah warns that later generations went astray and that repentance, faith, and righteous work lead to the Garden.
rows.anchor: These four accounts are followed by a brief mention of other prophetic figures

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah moves from revelation by God’s command to criticism of the Prophet and Quran, rejects claims God has a child, and ends with the silence of destroyed generations.
rows.anchor: After a reminder in v. 64 that revelation only comes to the Prophet by God’s Command, the sūrah proceeds to address the criticisms leveled against the Prophet and the Quranic message

none: Translation only; no commentary claims beyond the translated verse text.

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Commentators usually treat wudd, “love,” as synonymous with ḥubb, the Quran’s more usual word for love.
rows.anchor: Love here translates wudd, rather than ḥubb

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The common interpretation is that God grants believers and righteous people love in this world, especially among other believing servants.
rows.anchor: That God shall ordain love for those who believe and perform righteous deeds is understood to mean that God grants that such people will be loved in the world

rows.speaker: al-Sulamī
rows.claim: Al-Sulamī says righteous people are beloved by fellow Muslims, a manifestation of God’s love for them.
rows.anchor: Al-Sulamī states that such people are beloved by their fellow Muslims, which is none other than a manifestation of God’s Love for them

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī favors the interpretation that righteous believers are loved by others.
rows.anchor: Al-Rāzī favors this interpretation

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: An alternative interpretation is that God grants righteous believers what they themselves love; its proponents note that believers may be hated by disbelievers while some disbelievers are widely loved.
rows.anchor: some interpret the verse to mean that God will grant righteous believers what they love, rather than the state of being loved by others

rows.speaker: the hadith
rows.claim: A hadith supports the preferred view: when God loves a servant, He tells Gabriel to love that person, then Heaven and earth are moved to love them.
rows.anchor: when God loves a servant, He calls out to the Archangel Gabriel, “Verily I love so-and-so, so love him!”

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some say the verse consoled ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf, who worried about leaving his companions in Makkah.
rows.anchor: Some report that this verse was revealed as a consolation to ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf, who was concerned about leaving his companions in Makkah

rows.speaker: Shiite commentators
rows.claim: Shiite commentators understand the ordained love as love of and spiritual attachment to ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib; they hold only those who love ʿAlī to be true Muslim believers.
rows.anchor: For Shiite commentators, the love that God ordains for the righteous believers

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: A Shiite report says the Prophet told ʿAlī to ask God for a covenant and for love in believers’ hearts, after which this verse was revealed.
rows.anchor: According to a Shiite report, the Prophet said to ʿAlī

rows.speaker: some Sufis
rows.claim: Some Sufis understand the ordained love as unveiling divine secrets, linking it to a hadith qudsi in which God loves the servant who draws near through supererogatory acts.
rows.anchor: For some Sufis, the love that God ordains here is none other than the unveiling of Divine secrets

rows.speaker: al-Qushayrī
rows.claim: Al-Qushayrī cites a related hadith qudsi in which the servant draws near until he loves God and God loves him.
rows.anchor: Al-Qushayrī cites a similar ḥadīth: “My servant does not cease to draw nigh unto Me until he loves Me and I love him”

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Ṭā Hā is Makkan; some classify verses 130–131 as Madinan, but their context suggests they are Makkan.
rows.anchor: which some consider to be Madinan (JJ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah followed Maryam and figures in ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb’s conversion account: after reading its parchment at his sister’s house, he resolved to become Muslim and went to profess faith to the Prophet.
rows.anchor: resolved to become Muslim, and went to

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet reportedly said that God’s Supreme Name is found in this surah and in surahs 2 and 3.
rows.anchor: to be found in it (R)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah consoles the Prophet, recounts Moses and Adam, addresses the Last Day, urges steadfastness amid Makkan insults, and closes by warning the Makkans of the inevitable end.
rows.anchor: The sūrah begins with a consolation to the Prophet and speaks of God’s all-encompassing knowledge and His Most Beautiful Names
